note: The owner's record of what changed and where to see it. Every pull request that changes what a learner or the owner sees adds one entry at the top: the date, what changed in plain words, and links to the exact place to look. Shown at /owner/#changes.

entries.title: A repair is proven on new questions, not the same problem
entries.what: After a lesson, a hint or the worked solution, getting the same problem right no longer ends the recovery. The child might just remember it, or be lucky. The child now answers, alone, a new question of the same kind, then one in a slightly different form (for 126 ÷ 7: 406 ÷ 7, then a long-division word question). Where possible these use the same facts the problem needed, such as 7 × 8. Only when both come out right does it count as solved after help. After a wrong one, both start again. Two wrong means the gap isn't fixed yet, so it stops for a teacher or parent and counts nothing as solved. A plain second try with no help in between is unchanged. Child lab: 16 of 18 scenarios now handled, including a new child who remembers the answer to the problem without having learned it.

entries.title: Child lab: simulated children with real slips test every change
entries.what: 17 simulated children now go through the app on every change. Each makes a real step-level slip: a dropped minus sign, 7 × 8 = 54, adding without carrying, smaller-from-larger subtraction, 7² = 14, or guessing. One can't learn from lessons and one forgets after a week. They are not told what skill they lack; they work every question step by step, as a child would. A scenario the app handles must keep passing, or the change cannot go in. Today the app handles 14 of 17. The 3 known gaps are next on the plan: a new question to prove a repair, the same treatment both ways, and the Class 10 matrices links. The scorecard is on your owner view.

entries.title: Finding the exact step a child gets wrong
entries.what: When a child gets a problem wrong, OpenPath now checks the exact step that broke, not just the whole topic. For example, a Class 10 child who gets x² − 4x − 20 = 0 wrong because 4 × (−20) came out as +80 is now checked on multiplying negative numbers and taught it. Before, that step was filed under 'times tables', so the real gap was never found. If a skill is shown on the whole but the exact fact the problem needs (say 7 × 8 inside 126 ÷ 7) has not been answered right, the child gets one quick question on that fact. Two wrong on it means a lesson, then that fact is checked again. A topic is no longer marked as learned while the step it uses is known to be wrong. A first answer that was right after a hint or the worked solution now says 'Solved with help', never 'Solved on your own'.

entries.title: Class 1–3: numbers counted by what they mean, not by how the question reads
entries.what: Proposed, not live. A question's class now comes from the numbers its generator says it uses: quantities count, calendar years do not, and only real sequence questions are held to a growth limit. Digit cards (1, 5, 9), ₹10 for ₹6 and ₹2, a two-way table and a repeating 2, 5, 8 pattern go back to Class 1 (they were wrongly moved to Class 2 or 3 because their numbers happened to go up evenly). A ₹100 note in a coin picture, the ends of a number line the child reads, and estimates of 10,000 or more now count. 219 problems change class in all (657 screens).

links.label: Digit cards, greatest and smallest (child's view)

entries.title: The lift lesson: a lift to drag, steps coloured at 0, and pictures that stay
entries.what: In 'Jumps on the number line' the first picture is now the story's own lift. It shows a building cut open, with sky above floor 0 and earth below, and the child drags the lift down floor by floor with a tick on each floor. The steps down to 0 are orange and the steps past 0 are teal, so the picture shows 'three steps reach 0, two more go below it'. When the lift arrives, it turns on its side into the number line, and 'Show the lift' turns it back. Every jump on a number line in any lesson is now drawn step by step in the same two colours. A finished picture now stays on the page at its answer with 'Watch it again', instead of shrinking to one line. The guess now comes before the picture that answers it.

links.label: Add and subtract integers, Lesson (child's view)

entries.title: Class 3 rounding: real-life numbers a Class 3 child can work with
entries.what: Most rounding questions set in real situations (a truck's distance, a town's people, a shop's sales) used numbers in the ten-thousands to crores, which is Class 4 work and above. Class 3 children now get almost 300 of these questions with four-digit numbers (1,000 to 9,999), rounded to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand. For example: 'The number of people living in a town is 8,256. Round this number to the nearest ten.' The large-number questions are still there for Class 4 and up. Estimating a four-digit number times a two-digit number stays in Class 4, because its answers are above 9,999. Class 3 estimates products with smaller numbers instead.

entries.title: Class 1–3: numbers that fit the class, and short sentences
entries.what: Each Class 1–3 question now belongs to the class whose numbers it uses, following the CBSE, ICSE and Tamil Nadu books. Class 1 uses numbers up to 99 and patterns that grow by 1 or 2. Class 2 goes up to 999 and growth up to 10. Class 3 goes up to 9,999. A child is never asked a question above their class, so a Class 1 child gets 1, 3, 5, 7 … rather than 7, 10, 13 …. Years and dates don't count as big numbers. Lesson examples now use numbers from the class where the skill starts. All 84 long sentences in Class 1–3 lessons are rewritten into short ones of no more than 22 words, and a check keeps it that way.

entries.title: Lessons read plainly, and your view shows each lesson's picture
entries.what: Your maths view left out the picture a child sees, so 'The table shows a growing pattern of dots' appeared with no table. It now shows the same table or picture the child gets. The growing-pattern working now starts from the given numbers ('Step 1 has 7 and step 2 has 10, so the pattern grows by 3 each step', then 'Keep adding 3: 13, 16, 19') instead of 'From 7 to 10'. Every maths lesson sentence joined with a semicolon is now split into two short sentences. New checks stop a question from pointing at a picture it does not have, and stop long sentences in Class 1–3 lessons from increasing.

entries.title: Tap-the-picture cards: a wrong tap says what is off and which way to go
entries.what: On the 'On the picture' cards, a wrong tap used to repeat itself ('You chose row 1, column 2. That is the entry in row 1, column 2.'). Now it says what is off and which way to move: 'That is column 2. The row is right: you need column 3, 1 column to the right.' Points on a grid say the same: 'That is (2, 3). Go 1 step to the right, then 5 steps down.' Other pictures (circles, angles, Venn diagrams) keep naming the part tapped, without giving the answer away.

links.label: Matrices (Class 10): Start here, On the picture

entries.title: Changeable numbers only where changing them shows something
entries.what: 30 Start here screens lose their changeable numbers and go back to fixed examples (keeping their rewritten words). They felt locked: a number that could take only a few values, too few choices in all, tiles pulled out of the matrix onto a separate 'Change:' line, or a fixed picture showing the example's numbers that wouldn't follow them. The matrix inverse screen is one. 83 screens stay changeable. A new automatic rule keeps it that way for every screen.

links.label: Matrix inverse (Class 12): now a fixed example

entries.title: Change the numbers: explanations rewrite themselves
entries.what: In Start here, a number of the example sits in a soft tile. Tap it, type another, and the whole explanation is written again for it: the words, the steps, the check and the picture. The first time, the tiles pulse with 'Tap a number to change it'. Numbers that don't fit get a short note, and 'Back to the first numbers' returns to the example. 113 Start here screens across Classes 1–12 now work this way, their words rewritten to show first and name after; every possible choice of numbers (about 500,000) is checked automatically for true sums and complete sentences. In lessons, the pinned question's numbers are tiles too (where the question family allows), replacing the separate 'What if the numbers change?' box. What a child tries is saved to their record (not counted as mastery).

links.label: Linear equations lesson: tap a number of the pinned question

entries.title: Lessons: method on screen, Example and Scribble as buttons, question pinned
entries.what: Every child's lesson screen now shows only the method text at first. Two separate buttons stay at the bottom of the lesson: Example (the guess and the worked steps) and Scribble (the rough-work pad). Each one that is on turns blue with a tick, and both can be open together. When the example is open, its question (and its own picture, if it has one) stays pinned at the top while the steps scroll under it; 'Make smaller' shrinks it to one line. A screen with no method text opens on its example.

links.label: Solve pairs of linear equations: the new lesson screen

entries.title: Sorting buttons: tap them into glass jars
entries.what: Class 1 sorting is now the approved button design instead of sentences. Red and blue, big and small sewing buttons lie on a wooden table. The child taps Start; a finger shows one big button going into the jar ('one'), then 'Now you'. Each right tap flies a button into the jar and says the count; a wrong one shakes ('No. That one is small.'). Then 'red AND big' is sorted twice: all the red ones into jar 1, then the big ones out of those into jar 2 ('two buttons are red and big.'), with Again (under the jars, never over a button). Everything is spoken, lines never cut each other off, quick taps all count, and what to do is said again after 7 seconds of nothing. A sorting question's 'Break it down' in the lesson now shows the same sort with that question's own buttons, and 'there are 1' now reads 'there is 1'. Questions read aloud no longer end in a stray 'what' ("which are big what"). The 'Now you try' after it is now two more sorts with other buttons (one thing, then two), spoken, with no words to read; a sort with nothing refused counts as right the first time. 'Break it down' (the sort, and the lift) now scrolls the picture into view and starts it at once, so it is heard straight away; a reminder is cut short when the child taps.

links.label: Sorting by colour and size: Start here, Sort the buttons

entries.title: Absolute value: a live number line instead of a still picture
entries.what: In the polygon-area skill (Class 10–11), the Start here idea on the | | bars now has a number line the learner slides. A bar from 0 to the point shows its distance from 0 and reads |−4| = 4. The lift story and the 'removes a minus sign' shortcut are gone; the text now says plainly why the area formula needs the bars.

links.label: Polygon areas: Start here, The bars mean distance from 0

entries.title: The lift ride: Chintu in a building, a lift panel with big buttons
entries.what: The lift is now the approved design. A building cut open: floors above in sky blue, floor 0 is the gold shop, the car park (minus floors) below, only the floors the question needs. Chintu rides in the lift; the child taps Start and presses the big green up or orange down button once for every floor. Each press closes the doors, moves one floor, opens them with a ding and says the floor ('minus one'; 0 is 'zero. The shop.'). A finger shows the first press, then 'Now you.' The wrong button shakes: 'Down, not up.' Quick taps all count. After each move the sum so far shows and is said (3 − 5 = −2), and at the end the whole sum (3 − 5 + 4 = 2), with Again. Lines are no longer said on top of each other. Money and temperature keep the counter.

links.label: Class 1 adding: Start here, Ride the lift

entries.title: Count with me: a counting game for ages 3–6
entries.what: A new 'Count with me' tile on the home screen opens a self-contained counting game: 10 illustrated pages (floor tiles, meadow sheep, pond, garden, mango tree, sea, night sky, hen house, market, road), counting up to 3 on page 1 and up to 10 on page 10. Each page has five rounds: count every one, find only one kind, compare which group has more, make a number, and a quick look at up to 5. Numbers are spoken (English or Tamil), difficulty adapts to the child, a hint glows after 7 seconds, and a grown-ups panel on its first screen shows progress on this phone.

entries.title: Mango boxes: count, then put together on a ten-spot board
entries.what: Class 1 adding now opens with the approved mango picture. The child taps each mango in the first box, then the second (every number is said aloud), a finger shows one mango going onto a wooden board of ten spots, and the child moves the rest by tapping or dragging, the count going on: 1, 2, 3, +, 4, 5. It ends with '3 + 2 = 5', said as 'three plus two makes five.' A tap on the wrong box shakes it: 'First this box.' The lift for 3 + 2 follows as before.

links.label: Class 1 adding: Start here, Plus and equals

entries.title: The counter and the lift for young children
entries.what: On a Class 1–5 adding or taking-away question, 'Break it down' (above 'Work it with me') opens a lift. The child drops +/− tiles (₹ coins for money) and the counter clicks through every number, pausing at 0. Change is counted up from the price. The instruction is read aloud after the first tap. Class 1–3 see no written reasons, and each 'Work it with me' step now states its numbers.

links.label: Class 1 adding: Lesson, then Break it down
Class 1 taking away: Lesson, then Break it down

entries.title: Why? on every step of the generated lessons
entries.what: Each worked step in a lesson has a Why? button; Break it down opens them all. 1,110 of 1,119 question types have reasons. Each tap is recorded.

entries.title: Break it down on every Start here example (Class 1–12)
entries.what: Every worked example before a lesson is shown as steps, each with its own Why?.

entries.title: A taught lesson for tangents to an ellipse
entries.what: Five screens before the formula sheet: drag a point round an ellipse, one rule and why, every step written out, the normal. Twelve practice questions.

entries.title: Open as a child, from your dashboard
entries.what: Each skill in the dashboard has an 'Open as a child' link. The practice list is labelled as an answer key.

entries.title: Pictures for the ideas before a lesson, and older drawings moved into the engine
entries.what: 28 more Start here ideas have a picture; every idea either has one or says why not. All maths teaching pictures are drawn by the one picture engine.

entries.title: Start here is measured
entries.what: A finished Start here round is recorded and shown to the parent; a shaky idea is offered again before the chapter.
